Q993.L1t: The Seventh Amendment preserves the right to a jury trial in federal civil cases that are legal in nature, and Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 38 governs how that right is invoked.
Q993.L2t: Under Rule 38, a party can waive the right to a jury trial by failing to make a proper and timely demand.
Q993.L3t: Rule 38 lets a party demand a jury by serving a written demand no later than 14 days after the last pleading directed to the issue is served, and it also allows the demand to be made in a pleading itself.
Q993.L4t: The lawyer should include the jury demand in the complaint, which is filed and served at the start of the action, so the right is secured at the earliest possible point.
Q993.L2f: Patent infringement claims are equitable in nature, so federal courts historically tried them without a jury.
Q993.L3f: Under the federal rules, a jury demand is timely if it is raised orally with the court at the initial pretrial conference, since that is when the trial format is set.
Q993.L4f: The lawyer should wait and make the jury demand at the initial pretrial conference, because that is the proper time to secure a jury trial.

Q947.L1t: Pain is a subjective experience that is influenced by physical, emotional, and cultural factors, and it is a central concern in nursing and clinical care.
Q947.L2t: Pain assessment tools such as numeric rating scales and visual analogue scales were developed to help quantify what patients report about their pain.
Q947.L3t: Unlike blood pressure or temperature, pain has no laboratory test, scan, or instrument that can measure it directly, so clinicians have to depend on what the patient tells them.
Q947.L4t: The patient's self-report matters because staff have no objective way of measuring pain.
Q947.L2f: Pain scales are used only for patients who are unconscious, and conscious patients are never asked to rate their pain.
Q947.L3f: Studies consistently show that health care staff routinely rate a patient's pain as lower than the patient reports, which makes the patient's own rating necessary as a correction.
Q947.L4f: The patient's self-report matters because staff tend to underestimate how intense the patient's pain is.

Q992.L1t: Rape is a criminal offense defined by statute or common law, and the defenses available to a defendant depend on the mental state the offense requires.
Q992.L2t: Voluntary intoxication is a defense only to crimes that require a specific intent, and it is generally not a defense to crimes of general intent or recklessness.
Q992.L3t: Under the traditional rule, a defendant's mistaken belief that the victim consented can negate guilt only if the belief was honest and also reasonable, and the jury has found this belief was unreasonable.
Q992.L4t: The defendant should be found guilty because the victim did not consent and his belief that she consented was unreasonable.
Q992.L2f: At common law, rape required proof that the defendant specifically intended to cause the victim serious bodily harm.
Q992.L3f: A defendant who is voluntarily intoxicated is held only to the mental state he actually had, so intoxication may be used to negate any mental element, including the intent for general intent crimes.
Q992.L4f: The defendant should be found guilty because rape is a general intent crime, so his intoxication and honest belief do not matter.
